summary: Extends LSP ping to find faults in point-to-multipoint MPLS label switched paths. It does not replace existing LSP ping mechanisms but clarifies how they apply to the point-to-multipoint case. It updates RFC 4379.

plainLanguage.summary: LSP ping is the MPLS version of the familiar ping command: it sends a test packet along a label switched path to check that the path really carries traffic, and can trace where it breaks. This RFC makes that work for trees that fan out from one router to many.

subtitle: Extends LSP ping so it can test point-to-multipoint MPLS trees.

tldr.problem: A point-to-multipoint MPLS label switched path can fail silently, and the control plane does not always notice, so operators need a way to detect and isolate the fault.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the existing LSP ping echo request and reply messages with new TLVs that identify a point-to-multipoint LSP, let the initiator ask a single node to answer, and let responders stagger their replies.
tldr.outcome: A ping or traceroute over a multicast tree now works, with the replies controlled so that a tree with many leaves does not flood the ingress router.

sections.title: What LSP Ping Does and Why a Tree Needs It
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) label switched paths (LSPs) are tested by sending information in MPLS echo request and echo reply messages. Those messages carry enough information to check that the data plane is working, and to compare the data plane against the control plane, which is how a fault is localized. Using a reliable channel for the replies, as described in RFC 4379, makes the fault isolation more robust. This collection of mechanisms is commonly called LSP ping.

Point-to-point LSPs are covered by that document. Requirements for point-to-multipoint MPLS traffic engineered LSPs are stated in RFC 4461, and the signaling is in RFC 4875. The requirements for point-to-multipoint extensions to the Label Distribution Protocol are in RFC 6348, with the extensions themselves in RFC 6388.

A point-to-multipoint LSP is at least as vulnerable to data-plane faults and to disagreements between the control and data planes as a point-to-point one, so the same detection is needed. This document extends the existing LSP ping mechanisms rather than inventing new ones, which keeps implementation and operation simpler. One requirement carries over from the point-to-point case: the echo request must follow the same data path as the packets being tested, which for a tree means that the request is replicated so that it reaches every leaf.

Echo requests are meant to validate the data plane, and can then be used to compare it against the control plane. They may also bootstrap other operations, administration and maintenance procedures. Checking the liveness and consistency of the control plane itself is not a feature of LSP ping and is not covered here. As in RFC 4379, a rate limiter SHOULD be applied to the incoming LSP ping traffic, to limit the risk of denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: LSP ping sends a test packet down a labeled path to prove that traffic can still get through. In a tree, the test packet is copied to every branch, so each leaf can check its own path.

sections.title: The Test in a Point-to-Multipoint Tree
sections.content:
The basic idea of LSP ping is to test that the packets belonging to a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) actually end their path on a router that is an egress for that FEC. An MPLS echo request is sent along the same data path as the other packets of that FEC and carries information about the FEC being checked, and it is forwarded like any other packet of that FEC. In ping mode the packet should reach the end of the path, where the control plane of the egress router verifies that it is indeed an egress for the FEC. In traceroute mode the packet goes to the control plane of each transit router, which checks that it is a transit router for this path and returns information that helps compare forwarding with what the routing protocols decided.

Point-to-multipoint LSPs come in two flavours. A point-to-multipoint LDP LSP distributes data from a single source to one or more destinations along the next hops the routing protocols indicate, and each LSP is identified by an MPLS multicast FEC. A point-to-multipoint MPLS TE LSP can be seen as a tunnel with a single ingress and multiple egresses, explicitly routed through the network, and it has no FEC of its own.

For a tree, the test becomes: do packets entering the LSP at its ingress actually end their path on the routers that are the intended egresses? The idea can be extended to check that such packets reach one specific egress. The echo request is forwarded as any other packet using the LSP, so it is replicated at the branch points and should be delivered to all egresses. In ping mode the request reaches the end of the path, where the control plane of each egress verifies that it is indeed a leaf, and each egress sends a reply to the ingress confirming receipt or announcing an erroneous arrival. In traceroute mode the request is sent to the control plane at each transit router, which checks that it is a transit router for this LSP and returns information about the outgoing paths, which the ingress can use to build topology and downstream routers can use for extra label verification.

A tree may have many egresses, and the initiator may not want information about all of them. Pinging every egress of a large tree would send a large number of replies to the ingress at roughly the same time, which could congest it. The RFC gives two mechanisms to control the replies: responders may delay their replies at random, and the initiator may limit the scope of the request to one specific intended egress.
sections.plainLanguage: The test is simple: does a packet sent into the tree come out at the leaves where it should? Each leaf answers for itself, and the traceroute variant asks each router on the way to confirm that it is really on the path.

sections.title: Identifying the LSP Under Test
sections.content:
The basic structure of the LSP ping packet does not change from RFC 4379, but new TLVs and sub-TLVs are needed. To identify a point-to-multipoint MPLS TE LSP, the echo request MUST carry a Target FEC Stack TLV, and that TLV MUST carry exactly one of two new sub-TLVs: the RSVP P2MP IPv4 Session sub-TLV or the RSVP P2MP IPv6 Session sub-TLV. The sub-TLVs carry fields from the RSVP-TE P2MP SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE objects of RFC 4875, which together identify the LSP uniquely. Their sub-type numbers are 17 for the IPv4 session and 18 for the IPv6 session, with lengths of 20 and 56 bytes.

To identify a multicast LDP LSP, the echo request MUST again carry a Target FEC Stack TLV, and this MUST carry exactly one of the Multicast P2MP LDP FEC Stack sub-TLV or the Multicast MP2MP LDP FEC Stack sub-TLV. These use fields from the multicast LDP messages of RFC 6388. Their sub-type numbers are 19 and 20, and both have a variable length. Each carries an address family, the length of the root LSR address, the address of the LSR at the root of the tree, and an opaque value that identifies the LSP in the context of that root. If the address family is IPv4 the address length MUST be 4, and if it is IPv6 the length MUST be 16; no other address families are defined at present.

The same mechanisms extend to multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs. In such a tree any leaf can be treated like the head node of a point-to-multipoint tree, so the tree can be treated as a collection of point-to-multipoint trees, with each leaf acting as a head-end node and the remaining leaves acting as egress or bud nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The test packet has to say which path it is testing. Four new sub-TLVs do that: one for a traffic-engineered tree over IPv4, one for IPv6, and two for trees set up by the label distribution protocol.

sections.title: Limiting Which Nodes Reply
sections.content:
A new P2MP Responder Identifier TLV, type 11, is included in the echo request to control who answers. It has meaning only on an echo request and MUST be ignored on an echo reply. It carries zero or more sub-TLVs. If no sub-TLVs are present the TLV MUST be processed as if it were absent, and if more than one is present the first MUST be processed and the rest SHOULD be ignored.

Four sub-TLVs are defined. Sub-type 1 is an IPv4 Egress Address P2MP Responder of length 4, sub-type 2 an IPv6 Egress Address P2MP Responder of length 16, sub-type 3 an IPv4 Node Address P2MP Responder of length 4, and sub-type 4 an IPv6 Node Address P2MP Responder of length 16.

An Egress Address sub-TLV names the intended egress. A node that receives an echo request with this sub-TLV MUST respond if it lies on the path to that address, and MUST NOT respond otherwise. For this to work the address must be known to the nodes upstream in the LSP, which is the case when RSVP-TE signals the tree, because the address is then the one used in the destination address field of the S2L_SUB_LSP object. With Multicast LDP there is no way for upstream routers to know the identity of the downstream leaves, so these sub-TLVs cannot be used to trace to a single node and SHOULD NOT be used with an echo request that carries a Multicast LDP FEC Stack sub-TLV; a node that receives them there will not respond, because it cannot tell whether it lies on the path.

A Node Address sub-TLV names a node rather than a path. A node that receives an echo request with one of these sub-TLVs MUST respond if the address matches an address local to the node, and MUST NOT respond otherwise. The address may be any of the node's physical interfaces or its router ID. It SHOULD be the address of a transit, branch, bud or egress node of the tree, though the address of a node that is not on the tree may be used as a check that no reply comes back.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can name one router it wants to hear from. Routers that are not named stay silent, which keeps a test of one branch from producing answers from the whole tree.

sections.title: Jitter and the TTL Expired Flag
sections.content:
The Echo Jitter TLV, type 12, tells responders how long they may wait before replying. The jitter time field gives an upper bound in milliseconds, and a responding node MUST wait a random amount of time between zero and that value. The TLV has meaning only on an echo request and MUST be ignored on an echo reply. If the TLV is present the responder MUST apply the delay, and if it is absent the responding egress SHOULD NOT add any delay of its own, though it MAY delay according to local policy. Echo reply jittering SHOULD be used for point-to-multipoint LSPs, although it MAY be omitted for simple trees or when the Node Address sub-TLVs are used. The responding node MUST set the timestamp received fields before applying any delay.

LSP ping MUST NOT be used to measure round-trip time for data delivery, because these LSPs are unidirectional and the reply often travels back through the control plane. The timestamps MAY be used to deduce information about delivery times, for example their variance.

A new T flag, the Respond Only If TTL Expired flag, is added to the Global Flags field of RFC 4379. It MUST be set only by the sender in the echo request, MUST NOT be set in the echo reply, and MUST be ignored if it appears in one. If the flag is 0 the receiving node MUST process the request. If it is 1 and the TTL of the incoming MPLS label is 1, the node MUST process the request; if the TTL is more than 1 the node MUST drop the request and MUST NOT reply. If the flag is 1 and the request carries no incoming MPLS labels, a bud node with PHP configured MAY choose not to respond, and all other nodes MUST ignore the bit and respond normally.
sections.plainLanguage: Two knobs control the flood of replies. One spreads them out in time so the sender is not hit all at once. The other makes a router answer only when the test packet was meant to expire there.

sections.title: How the Nodes Respond
sections.content:
The initiating router follows the procedures of RFC 4379 and puts a Target FEC Stack TLV with one of the new sub-TLVs in the echo request. It may limit the replies to a single egress with the P2MP Responder Identifier TLV, or omit that TLV to ask all egresses to answer. It may also ask for jittered replies, because a large tree would otherwise deliver many replies at once and could swamp the initiating router or exceed a rate limit. The bounds of the jitter should be under the sender's control, since a small tree needs little jitter and a large one needs more.

The responding router rate-limits incoming echo requests, checks the general sanity of the packet, and follows the RFC 4379 procedures if the packet is malformed or a TLV is not understood. For a point-to-multipoint ping or traceroute, the responding router MUST check with the control plane whether it is part of the tree. If it is not, it MUST respond according to RFC 4379. If it is, and a P2MP Responder Identifier TLV is present, the node follows the rules for those sub-TLVs to decide whether to answer; if the TLV is absent, or present but empty, the node MUST respond according to RFC 4379.

Return codes say what the reply means. A transit or branch node may report success with return code 8, label switched at stack-depth, and a branch node includes one Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV for each downstream path it reports. An egress node reports success with return code 3, replying router is an egress for the FEC at stack-depth, and includes no Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV. A bud node, which can be an egress, a transit node or both, decides by the responder identifier it receives: with no responder identifier it behaves as a combination of egress and branch node; with a Node Address sub-TLV it behaves the same way if the address matches one of its own, and sends no reply if it does not; with an Egress Address sub-TLV it behaves as an egress only if the address matches, as a transit node if it lies on the path, and sends no reply otherwise.

Traceroute needs extra care. A reply from one egress does not end the trace, because there may be deeper nodes, so the RFC recommends a configurable upper limit on the TTL values so the operator chooses how deep to probe. For a traffic-engineered LSP the initiator knows the number of egresses and their addresses, so it can continue until each has answered. For a Multicast LDP LSP it may not know them all, so there may be no definitive end to the trace. The Respond Only If TTL Expired flag is recommended for point-to-multipoint traceroute to stop bud and egress nodes answering repeatedly, though it does not help where PHP is used, because then no labels reach those nodes. When no reply arrives, the next request with a larger TTL SHOULD be sent to trace further, though the ingress MAY stop there.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router that receives the test packet checks whether it is part of the tree and whether it was asked to answer, then replies with a code that says what role it played. The sender keeps increasing the hop limit until it has heard from as much of the tree as it asked for.

sections.title: Routers That Do Not Comply and Day-to-Day Use
sections.content:
If a node on the tree does not support MPLS LSP ping, it sends no reply, which gives the initiating router a wrong result. There is no protection against this, so operators may want to make sure that every node on the tree supports the function. If the node that does not comply is an egress, the traceroute mode can still verify the LSP nearly all the way to the egress, leaving the final hop to be checked by hand. If it is a branch or transit node, ping mode is not affected, but that node will not answer during a traceroute.

Several points matter for running this in a live network. Scaling is the first one: only cautious use of LSP ping is advised, because sending a ping to all the egresses of a tree can congest the ingress when the replies arrive, and using timers to generate echo requests, especially in traceroute mode, can significantly degrade network performance. Management interfaces should give the operator full control over the operation of LSP ping, including the ability to limit the scope of a request to a single egress, and the ability to disable all active LSP ping operations as a quick escape when the network becomes congested. A MIB module is required for the control and management of LSP ping operations and for inspecting the reported information, and the RFC sees no reason why this should not be a simple extension of the LSP ping MIB module used for point-to-point LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Ping the whole tree and every leaf answers at once, which can overload the router that started the test. The RFC therefore asks for caution, for a way to test one branch, and for a switch to turn the whole function off quickly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no security concerns beyond those already described in RFC 4379. It does add one warning. Because a point-to-multipoint LSP can have many egresses, there is a stronger concern about regulating the LSP ping traffic passed to the control plane, using a rate limiter applied to the LSP ping well-known UDP port. That rate limiting might in turn lead to false indications of LSP failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is introduced, but a tree with many leaves produces many more replies, so the rate limiter on the ping port matters more here. Too tight a limit can make a healthy path look broken.

viz.caption: PING MODE ON A POINT-TO-MULTIPOINT TREE (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC)

messages.label: MPLS echo request
messages.note: Follows the data path of the tree and is replicated at branch points.

messages.label: MPLS echo reply
messages.note: Return code 3: the replying router is an egress for the FEC.

messages.label: MPLS echo reply
messages.note: Return code 8: label switched at stack-depth, in traceroute mode.

viz.caption: RSVP P2MP IPV4 SESSION SUB-TLV VALUE FIELD

fields.name: Tunnel ID
fields.desc: Tunnel identifier from the SENDER_TEMPLATE object.

fields.name: IPv4 Tunnel Sender Address
fields.desc: Address of the ingress that set up the tree.

items.label: IPv4 Egress Address
items.desc: Name the egress to trace to. Only nodes on the path to it reply.

items.label: IPv4 Node Address
items.desc: Name one node. Only that node replies.

viz.caption: THE ROLES A ROUTER CAN PLAY IN THE TREE

items.title: Ingress
items.text: Starts the echo request and collects the replies.

items.title: Transit
items.text: Carries the request and, in traceroute mode, checks that it is on the path.

items.title: Branch
items.text: Splits the tree, so the request is replicated from there on.

items.title: Bud
items.text: End of one branch and inside another, so it may answer as egress, transit or both.

items.title: Egress
items.text: Leaf of the tree. It checks that it is an egress and replies with return code 3.
